title: There IS Proof Knowledge Works. And It's Overwhelming.
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Pondiscio answers a Hechinger Report column claiming there has never been a study showing that increasing knowledge boosts reading scores. He calls the claim misleading, arguing the real issue is the difficulty of isolating long-term curricular effects, since gains accumulate over years while most studies run weeks or months. He rejects the caricature that knowledge-rich curricula force children to memorise facts, citing Willingham, Wiliam, the baseball study and a meta-analysis on strategy instruction. He ties the case to his idea of cargo cult reading, in which students imitate what good readers do without knowing what they know. He closes with the Core Knowledge study, including its low-income school, and Hirsch's equity argument against segregated knowledge.
points: The absence of a perfect causal study reflects the limits of research methods, not the weakness of the case for knowledge.
Effects of knowledge-building curricula accrue over years, and the research needed is expensive and slow.
The proposed analogy to smoking and cancer, and to diet and exercise, shows we accept cumulative evidence in other fields.
Teaching what good readers do produces cargo cult reading, whereas a knowledge-rich curriculum instils what good readers know.
Knowledge-rich curriculum is an equity measure because disadvantaged children lack the knowledge advantaged peers acquire at home.
quotes: Such a broad and sweeping statement is demonstrably incorrect, deeply misleading, and carries significant downside for reading instruction if taken uncritically. The issue is not a lack of compelling evidence—there is prodigious evidence—but rather the difficulty of isolating long-term curricular effects in research.

A useful comparison can be drawn to dieting and exercise. It might be challenging to show a direct cause-and-effect relationship between a specific weight loss and exercise program, but that does not mean the broader evidence for diet and exercise is lacking. We accept that long-term health outcomes are influenced by consistent, cumulative behaviors.

Valorizing knowledge-rich curricula is a sensible response to decades spent focusing on reading “skills and strategies” that demonstrably fail to transfer to new and unfamiliar contexts. Recent meta-analytical research also suggests (not surprisingly) that the effects of reading strategy instruction is significantly strengthened by instruction in background knowledge (Peng et al., 2023).

A knowledge-rich curriculum is not about privileging certain students but about ensuring that all students—regardless of background—have access to the cultural and intellectual capital needed to engage fully in civic and professional life.
